The metaphor is beautifully literal: to ~depender~ is to “hang from” something, exactly as a ~pendiente~ (“earring, pendant”) hangs from an ear. What hangs from a support is held up by it and cannot stand alone — so “hanging from” became “being contingent upon,” relying on. The same ~pendēre~ family gave Spanish ~pender~, ~pendiente~, ~suspender~, ~depender~, and ~independiente~. And here is the surprise: the frequentative ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), from the same root, split into two Spanish verbs — ~pesar~ (“to weigh”) and ~pensar~ (“to think”) — because to weigh an idea in the mind is to think it over. So ~depender~, ~pesar~, and ~pensar~ all hang, in the end, from the same thread.
en.desarrollar:
A Spanish formation from ~des-~ (a prefix of reversal) and ~arrollar~ (“to roll up”), which is ~a-~ plus ~rollo~ (“a roll, scroll”). ~rollo~ descends from Latin ~rotulus~ (“little wheel, roll”), the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The wheel-root has far-flung cognates: German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), and Old Irish ~roth~ (“wheel”); ~rotulus~ itself gave English ~roll~ and ~role~ through French ~rôle~.

The image is vivid and exact: to develop is literally to un-roll — ~des-~ + ~arrollar~ — as one opens a rolled scroll to reveal what is written inside. Growth, in this metaphor, is a scroll unspooling. English ~develop~ carries the very same picture by a different route (Old French ~desveloper~, “to unwrap”), so the two languages independently imagine progress as undoing a wrapping. From the same wheel-root Spanish keeps ~rollo~, ~arrollar~, ~rueda~ (“wheel,” straight from ~rota~), ~rótula~ (“kneecap”), and the borrowed ~rotación~ and ~control~ (via the roll-counter of French ~contre-rôle~).
en.descubrir:
From ~des-~ (a reversative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) plus ~cubrir~ (“to cover”), which comes from Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover completely”), a compound of ~co-~ (intensive) and ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”). ~Operīre~ derives from Proto-Italic *~opweriō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, shut”). The formation matches Old French ~descovrir~, whence English ~discover~; compare Italian ~scoprire~ and Portuguese ~descobrir~.

The morphology is beautifully transparent: to ~descubrir~ is literally to un-cover, to take the lid off — and Spanish uses it both for physically uncovering and for the mental act of discovery, exactly as English ~discover~ pairs with ~cover~. Columbus’s ~descubrimiento~ of America is the same word as lifting a cloth. From the ~cubrir~ family come ~cubierta~, ~cobertura~, ~encubrir~ and ~recubrir~, while the reversative ~des-~ productively negates hundreds of Spanish verbs.
en.desear:
From Latin ~dēsīderāre~ (“to long for, miss, feel the want of”), traditionally analyzed as ~dē-~ + ~sīdus~ (stem ~sīder-~, “star, constellation”), and inherited by Old Spanish as ~desear~. Cognate with Italian ~desiderare~ and Portuguese ~desejar~, and — through the noun ~dēsīderium~ — with English ~desire~ (via Old French).

The star etymology is the classic account, pairing ~dēsīderāre~ with ~cōnsīderāre~ (“to observe the stars closely”): to desire would be to note a star’s absence, to long for what is no longer in sight. But this is disputed — some scholars reject the ~sīdus~ connection outright and derive the verb from a root meaning “stretch, survey,” so the celestial story, charming as it is, should be taken as one proposal, not settled fact. Secure descendants include ~deseo~, ~deseable~ and ~desiderátum~; from ~sīdus~ itself come ~sideral~ and ~considerar~.
en.destacar:
A comparatively late loan: Spanish took ~destacar~ from French ~détacher~ (“to detach”), from Old French ~destachier~, the negative counterpart of ~atachier~ (“to attach”). French itself leaned on Italian ~staccare~ / ~distaccare~ (“to separate”), the antonym of ~attaccare~ (“to attach, join battle”). At the base lies a Germanic (Frankish) *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), the same source that gave Spanish ~estaca~ (“stake”). It entered Spanish dictionaries around 1705, cognate with English ~detach~.

The oldest sense was military: to ~destacar~ was to detach a body of troops from the main force. From “separate a part from the whole” grew the figurative “stand out, be conspicuous” — that which is set apart draws the eye. The very pair survives elsewhere in Spanish: ~atacar~ (“to attack”), taken from the ~attaccare~ side of the same Italian opposition, once meant “to join, engage.” Modern relatives include ~destacamento~ (“military detachment”), ~destacado~ (“prominent, outstanding”) and the shared ~estaca~.
en.detener:
From ~de-~ (“away, down”) joined to ~tener~, which comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”); the Latin verb rests on Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), holding being understood as keeping something taut. It is cognate with Italian ~tenere~, French ~tenir~ and Portuguese ~ter~, and — through the same root — with English ~tenant~, ~tenure~ and ~contain~.

Latin ~dētinēre~ meant “to hold back, keep back,” and Spanish ~detener~ inherited exactly that: to stop something in its course, and by a natural step to arrest — which is why a person taken into custody is a ~detenido~. The reflexive ~detenerse~ softened to “to pause, to linger over.” The “hold” family is one of Spanish's densest — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~mantener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while the underlying “stretch” sense surfaces in relatives like ~tenso~ and ~tienda~, a “tent” of stretched cloth.
en.determinar:
Spanish ~determinar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dētermināre~ (“to set bounds, mark off”), a compound of ~dē-~ (here intensive) and ~termināre~ (“to limit”), a verb on the noun ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit”). ~terminus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~termnos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~térmn̥~ (“boundary marker”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~τέρμα~ (térma, “goal, turning-post”) and ~τέρμων~ (térmōn, “border”). English took the same Latin word as ~determine~; ~term~ and ~terminal~ share the root.

The metaphor at the heart of the verb is spatial: to ~determinar~ is to draw a line around something, and by fixing its edges to fix what it is — hence the senses “to establish,” “to decide,” and “to cause.” The boundary was no small matter to the Romans: ~Terminus~ was a god, the deity of boundary stones, whose markers were sacred and whose festival, the ~Terminalia~, was kept each February. From the same root Spanish inherited ~término~ (“term, end”), ~terminar~ (“to finish”), ~terminal~, ~exterminar~, ~interminable~, and ~determinación~. To determine something, then, is to give it a ~terminus~ — an end that defines its beginning.
en.dirigir:
Spanish ~dirigir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dīrigere~ (“to set straight, guide, direct”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, rule, guide”). ~regere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct, rule”), one of the most productive of all roots, cognate with Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), Sanskrit ~rājan~ (“king”), German ~recht~ (“right”), and English ~right~ itself. French ~diriger~ and Italian ~dirigere~ are the Romance parallels.

The literal image is a straight line: to ~dirigir~ is to make something go straight toward a target — hence “to aim,” “to guide,” “to address (a letter),” and “to conduct or manage” an orchestra, a company, a film. Its popularly inherited cousin ~aderezar~ (“to season, to garnish, to set right”), worn smooth by ordinary transmission from the same Latin stock, stands beside the bookish, near-intact ~dirigir~. From ~regere~ and its root Spanish drew a rich harvest: ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~dirección~, ~director~, ~corregir~ (“to correct,” literally “to set right again”), ~erigir~, ~recto~ (“straight”), ~regla~ (“rule”), ~región~, and — presiding over them all — ~rey~ (“king”).
en.diseñar:
A Renaissance borrowing from Italian ~disegnare~ (“to draw, to design”), which itself continues Latin ~dēsignāre~ (“to mark out, trace, designate”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“out, down”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from the noun ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). It is cognate with French ~dessiner~ and English ~design~, and — from the same Latin verb by a learned path — with Spanish's own ~designar~.

Here lies a neat doublet. Latin ~dēsignāre~ reached Spanish twice: once directly from Latin as the learned ~designar~ (“to appoint, designate”), and once through Italian, where ~disegnare~ had narrowed to the artist's act of “drawing, laying out a design” — that borrowing became ~diseñar~, with the noun ~diseño~. So a single Latin verb split into “to designate” and “to design.” The base ~signum~ radiates through Spanish in ~signo~, ~señal~, ~seña~, ~insignia~ and even ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), literally to “mark out” something for a learner.
en.disfrutar:
Spanish ~disfrutar~ was formed within Spanish itself from the prefix ~dis-~ and ~fruto~ (“fruit, produce”), with the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~fruto~ comes from Latin ~frūctus~ (“fruit, produce, profit”), the past participle of the deponent verb ~fruī~ (“to enjoy, have the use of”). That verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰruHg-~ (“to make use of, enjoy”). The root surfaces widely: Latin ~frūx~ (“crop, fruit”) gave ~frūgālis~, source of English ~frugal~; and through the Germanic branch it yielded English ~brook~ (the verb “to tolerate, put up with,” originally “to make use of, enjoy”) and German ~brauchen~ (“to need, use”). French ~fruit~ and Portuguese ~fruto~ / ~desfrutar~ are close Romance kin.

The metaphor is agricultural: to ~disfrutar~ something was first to draw the fruits or profit from it — to reap the yield of an estate — and only afterward to enjoy it in the modern sense of taking pleasure. Old legal Spanish kept the concrete meaning of usufruct, the right to gather another’s produce, and the doublet ~usufructo~ still names it in law. Today ~disfrutar de la vida~ (“to enjoy life”) has fully abstracted the harvest into pleasure. From the same ~fruto~ family Spanish holds ~fruta~, ~fructífero~ (“fruitful”), ~usufructo~, and ~frugal~; the learned ~fruición~ (“keen enjoyment”) comes straight from ~fruī~’s participle ~fruitus~.
en.disponer:
Spanish ~disponer~ continues Latin ~dispōnere~ (“to arrange, set in order, distribute”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~pōnere~ (“to place, put”). ~pōnere~ is itself contracted from an older ~po-~ (a by-form of the prefix meaning “away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), so its literal weight is “to set down, put in place.” The Romance cognates are exact — Italian ~disporre~, French ~disposer~, Portuguese ~dispor~ — and English ~dispose~ arrived through Old French.

The prefix ~dis-~ paints the picture: to ~disponer~ is to place things about, each in its own spot — hence “to arrange” and, from having things arranged and ready, “to have at one’s disposal.” The reflexive ~disponerse a~ means to get ready to do something. ~pōnere~ is one of the great Latin verb-factories, and Spanish reflects it everywhere: ~poner~ (“to put”), ~componer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~, ~suponer~, ~posición~, ~puesto~, and the derived noun ~disposición~ (“arrangement, disposal, willingness”). The adjective ~disponible~ (“available”) carries the same idea — something set out and ready to hand.
en.elaborar:
From Latin ~ēlabōrāre~ (“to work out, produce by effort”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~labōrāre~ (“to labor, toil”), from the noun ~labor~ (“labor, hardship”). It is cognate with French ~élaborer~, Italian ~elaborare~, and Portuguese ~elaborar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~elaborate~ and ~laborious~.

The origin of ~labor~ itself is uncertain: it has been proposed that it is related to ~labāre~ (“to totter, slip”), from the image of a body swaying under a heavy burden, but this is not established. The prefix ~ex-~ lent an intensive “thoroughly” force, so ~ēlabōrāre~ meant to work something out fully — hence the modern “to elaborate, produce.” The verb ~labōrāre~ left two Spanish descendants: the patrimonial ~labrar~ (“to till, work the land”) and the learned ~laborar~. The same family gave ~laboratorio~, ~colaborar~, ~laborioso~, and ~laborable~, all circling the ancient Roman sense of sustained, hard work.
en.elegir:
From Latin ~ēligere~ (“to pick out, to choose”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”). ~legere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~legō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), the ancestor of ~-logy~ and ~logic~. Old Spanish inherited the verb as ~esleer~/~eslecher~ before the learned ~elegir~ reshaped it on the Latin model. Cognate with Italian ~eleggere~, French ~élire~, and Portuguese ~eleger~.

~legere~ began concretely — to gather up, as one gathers olives or firewood — and then specialized in two directions: to gather written signs with the eye (“to read”) and to gather out the best (“to choose,” with ~ex-~). Spanish ~elegir~ keeps only the choosing sense, and its past participle ~electo~ gave the political ~elección~ and ~electorado~. The gathering root *~leǵ-~ also seeded ~leer~ (“to read”), ~colegio~, ~coleccionar~, ~legión~, and ~inteligente~ (“one who chooses between,” ~inter-~ + ~legere~).
en.elevar:
From Latin ~elevāre~ (“to lift up, raise”), from ~ex-~ (“out, up”) and ~levāre~ (“to lighten, to raise”), a verb built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”); the root reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“lightweight”). It is cognate with Italian ~elevare~ and French ~élever~, and — through the same root — with English ~elevate~, ~lever~ and even ~light~ itself.

The striking fact is that Latin ~levāre~ left Spanish two verbs at once. ~Elevar~ is the learned borrowing, taken from books with its ~-l-~ intact and its “raise, lift” sense; but the same verb, inherited by mouth through the centuries, became the wholly ordinary ~llevar~, its ~l-~ palatalised to ~ll-~ and its meaning drifted from “to lift” to “to carry, to take.” The two are twins from one source. Around them cluster ~elevación~, ~elevador~, ~relieve~ and, straight from ~levis~, the adjectives ~leve~ and ~liviano~ and the verb ~aliviar~ (“to lighten, relieve”).
en.eliminar:
From Latin ~ēlimināre~ (“to turn out of doors, expel, banish”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~līmen~ (“threshold, doorway”). The word thus literally meant to put someone out across the threshold — to show them the door. It is cognate with French ~éliminer~, Italian ~eliminare~, and Portuguese ~eliminar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~eliminate~.

From that concrete image of a doorway the sense broadened to “remove, get rid of, do away with.” The noun ~līmen~ (“threshold”) stands beside ~līmes~ (“boundary, path”), source of Spanish ~límite~; whether the two are the same word is itself debated, so the link is best left open. The prefix ~prae-~ (“before”) joined ~līmen~ in ~preliminar~, literally something standing “before the threshold” of a matter. In modern Spanish the verb gave the everyday ~eliminación~ and, from sport and competitions, ~eliminatoria~ (“qualifying round”).
en.empezar:
Spanish ~empezar~ is a compound of the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the noun ~pieza~ (“piece”) — some accounts reconstruct an intervening Vulgar Latin *~impettiāre~, though that form is only proposed, not attested. What is clear is the ~pieza~ at its core, and ~pieza~ is not Latin: it comes from Late Latin ~pettia~, borrowed from Gaulish *~pettyā~, from Proto-Celtic *~kʷezdis~. So one of Spanish's common verbs for “to begin” has a Celtic heart. Its Romance kin through ~pieza~ include French ~pièce~, Italian ~pezza~ and Portuguese ~peça~.

The image behind ~empezar~ is concrete and homely: to begin something is to break into it — to break off the first ~pieza~, to broach a whole. You start a loaf or a task by taking the first piece of it. From the same Celtic-derived ~pieza~ Spanish built ~despiezar~ (“to dismantle, to break into pieces”) and the noun ~empiece~ (“a beginning”), while ~pieza~ itself ranges from a coin to a room to a musical or theatrical piece. It is a small monument to the Gaulish substrate embedded in everyday Castilian.
en.encontrar:
From Vulgar Latin *~incontrāre~ (“to meet, to come up against”), a verb built from Latin ~in-~ (“in, upon”) plus ~contrā~ (“against, facing”), itself from ~cum~ / ~com-~ (“with”). Old Spanish inherited it as ~encontrar~. Its Romance relatives include Italian ~incontrare~, Portuguese ~encontrar~, and French ~encontrer~ (surviving today mainly in ~rencontrer~, “to meet”); English borrowed the same formation as ~encounter~ and, more plainly, ~counter~.

The literal core is confrontational — to come face to face, even against one another — but Spanish softened the edge: ~encontrar~ is now the neutral, everyday verb both for meeting a person and for finding a thing (« no encuentro las llaves »). The reflexive ~encontrarse~ adds “to be located” and “to feel” (« me encuentro bien »). From the same stem come the noun ~encuentro~ (“a meeting, a match”), the blunt ~encontronazo~ (“a collision, a run-in”), and, through the shared ~contrā~, a whole regiment of words — ~contra~, ~contrario~, ~encontrado~ (“opposing, conflicting”), and ~contrariar~.
en.enfrentar:
From ~en-~ (“in, into”) plus ~frente~ (“forehead; front”) and the verbal ending ~-ar~ — a verb built directly on the noun. ~frente~ descends from Latin ~frontem~, accusative of ~frons~ (“forehead, brow, front”), whose ultimate origin is uncertain; De Vaan finds “no plausible etymology”. The Latin noun lives on in Italian ~fronte~, French ~front~ and Portuguese ~frente~, and English ~front~ is its doublet, borrowed through Old French.

In Latin ~frons~ named the forehead and, by an easy metaphor, the foremost part of anything, including an army's front line — the sense that powers military ~frente~. Spanish keeps both meanings and even sorts them by gender: ~la frente~ is the forehead, ~el frente~ the front. To ~enfrentar~ is literally to set foreheads or fronts against each other, hence “to confront, to face”. From the same root grew ~frontera~ (“frontier”), ~afrontar~, ~confrontar~ and ~frontal~, while English gained ~frontier~ and ~confront~ along the way.
en.entender:
From Latin ~intendere~ (“to stretch toward, direct, aim at”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”). It is cognate with Italian ~intendere~, Portuguese ~entender~ and French ~entendre~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~intend~; the bare root shows up in English ~tend~ and ~thin~.

The Latin phrase ~intendere animum~ meant “to direct the mind toward” something; that mental aiming narrowed from “pay attention” to “grasp, understand.” A neat contrast: French ~entendre~ took the same verb and settled on “to hear” instead. The root *~ten-~ is remarkably fertile in Spanish: besides ~atender~ (“to attend to”) and ~intención~, it yields ~tensión~, the Greek-derived ~tono~, and — unexpectedly — ~tienda~ (“shop; tent”), originally a “stretched” awning under which goods were sold.
en.entrar:
Spanish ~entrar~ comes, through Old Spanish ~entrar~, from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to go in, enter”), a verb built on ~intrā~ (“within, inside”). ~intrā~ is the feminine ablative of an adjective going back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁énteros~ (“inner”), a comparative formed from *~h₁én~ (“in”) with the contrastive suffix *~-teros~. The word thus meant, quite literally, to move into the more-inner space. English ~enter~ (borrowed through Old French ~entrer~) and Italian ~entrare~ are close relatives, as are Portuguese and Catalan ~entrar~.

The Latin sense was concrete and spatial, and Spanish ~entrar~ keeps that physical core — to enter a room, a country, a stage — while branching into countless idioms: ~entrar en razón~ (“to see reason”), ~entrar en calor~ (“to warm up”), the new year that ~entra~. From the same ~intrā~/~inter~ stock Spanish holds ~entrada~ (“entrance, ticket”), ~entrante~ (“incoming; starter course”), and ~adentro~; the sister preposition ~inter~ underlies ~interior~, ~íntimo~, and ~entre~ (“between”) itself. The comparative shape of *~h₁énteros~ — “more inward” — reminds us that Latin often located actions not just in space but along a scale of depth.
en.entregar:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, renew, restore”), a verb built on the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, untouched, intact”), which is itself ~in-~ (“not”) plus the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”) — literally “untouched.” The Proto-Indo-European root is *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch, handle”). ~Entregar~ is a semi-learned descendant that underwent metathesis (~integrāre~ → ~entregar~); its fully learned doublet is ~integrar~ (“to integrate”). The pair is cognate with Portuguese ~entregar~, Italian ~integrare~ and English ~integrate~ and ~integer~.

The semantic path is unexpected. Latin ~integrāre~ meant to make something whole again, to restore it; Old Spanish ~entregar~ first meant to give back or restore what was owed, and from “to hand back” it slid to the general “to hand over, deliver” it means today. So the modern act of delivering a parcel hides an older idea of restoring something to wholeness. From the same ~tangere~ Spanish also has ~tangible~, ~tañer~ (“to play an instrument, to ring”), ~contacto~ and ~intacto~ (“untouched”), while ~integer~ lives on in ~íntegro~ (“whole, upright”) and ~entrega~ (“delivery, devotion”).
en.enviar:
Spanish ~enviar~ comes from Old Spanish ~enviar~, from Late Latin ~inviāre~ (“to send on a journey, dispatch”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~via~ (“way, road”). To ~inviāre~ was literally to put someone or something ~in viam~ — “on the road.” ~via~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weǵʰ-~ (“to go, transport in a vehicle”), one of the great roots of the family: it gave Latin ~vehere~ (“to carry”) and English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~, and ~wagon~, plus the borrowings ~via~, ~vehicle~, and ~voyage~. French ~envoyer~ is the exact cognate — and English ~envoy~ (“a messenger”) is simply its past participle ~envoyé~ borrowed whole.

The metaphor is transparent and durable: sending is still, etymologically, a matter of setting something on its way. From ordinary dispatch Spanish extended ~enviar~ to letters, messengers, goods, and now email and messages (~enviar un correo~, “to send an email”). A quirk of stress splits its present tense — the accent falls on the ~i~ in ~envío~ and ~envías~ but not in ~enviamos~ — a hiatus Spanish marks with a written accent. The verb’s own nouns are ~envío~ (“shipment, dispatch”) and ~enviado~ (“envoy, correspondent”). From the same ~via~ Spanish also keeps ~vía~, ~viaje~, ~enviar~’s cousin ~desviar~ (“to divert”), ~obvio~ (“obvious,” literally “in the way”), and ~trivial~ (from ~trivium~, “a place where three roads meet”).
en.escribir:
Spanish ~escribir~ descends from Latin ~scrībere~ (“to write”), whose original sense was “to scratch, to incise.” It goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to cut”), an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut,” also behind English ~shear~). Its native cognate is Greek ~skáriphos~ (“a scratching, an outline”). Tellingly, Germanic had no inherited verb for writing and simply borrowed this one from Latin — so German ~schreiben~ and Old English ~shrive~ are early loans, not true cognates. Romance kin include Italian ~scrivere~ and French ~écrire~.

The etymology preserves the physical act: to write was to gouge marks into wax, clay or stone with a stylus long before it meant putting ink to paper. From ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited a large family: ~escritura~ (“writing; Scripture; a legal deed”), ~escritor~ (“writer”), the participle ~escrito~ (“written; a document”), and the prefixed verbs ~describir~ (“to describe”) and ~inscribir~ (“to inscribe”), plus ~manuscrito~ (“manuscript,” literally hand-written).
en.escuchar:
From Old Spanish ~ascuchar~ (also ~escuchar~), from Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, a metathesis of Latin ~auscultāre~ (“to listen, give ear to”). The verb was built on the stem of ~auris~ (“ear,” from *~aus-~) plus a second element from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱlew-~ (“to hear”); by another account the second piece is *~ḱel-~ (“to incline”), itself linked to *~ḱlew-~. Romance kept the word everywhere: French ~écouter~, Italian ~ascoltare~, Portuguese ~escutar~.

The sound history is memorable: Latin ~auscultāre~ shed its heavy cluster through metathesis to Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, and the initial ~au-~ opened to ~e-~, yielding ~escuchar~. Centuries later the medical verb ~auscultar~ (“to listen to the chest”) was borrowed afresh straight from Latin, so Spanish keeps a doublet: everyday ~escuchar~ beside learned ~auscultar~, both literally “to lend an ear.” Many speakers preserve an aspectual contrast between ~oír~ (“to hear,” passive) and ~escuchar~ (“to listen,” attentive). From the same “ear” root come ~auricular~ and, of course, ~auscultar~.
en.esperar:
From Old Spanish ~esperar~, from Latin ~spērāre~ (“to hope”), a verb built on the noun ~spēs~ (“hope”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~speh₁-~ (“to thrive, prosper”). Cognate with Italian ~sperare~, French ~espérer~, and Portuguese ~esperar~, and — through the same Latin stem — with English ~prosper~, ~desperate~, and ~despair~, this last from ~dēspērāre~ (“to lose hope”).

As with ~estar~ and ~escuela~, Spanish grew a prothetic ~e-~ before the awkward ~sp-~ cluster, turning ~spērāre~ into ~esperar~. More striking is a semantic merger unusual among the big Romance languages: ~esperar~ carries both “to hope” and “to wait, expect,” so the same verb that voices optimism also names the patience it demands — context and prepositions do the sorting, as in ~esperar a~ someone (wait) versus ~esperar que~ something happen (hope). The root flowered into ~esperanza~ (“hope”), ~espera~ (“a wait”), and the darker ~desesperar~ and ~desesperado~ (“to despair”; “desperate”), alongside ~inesperado~ (“unexpected”).
en.establecer:
From Old Spanish ~establecer~, from Latin ~stabilīre~ (“to make firm, to establish”), a verb from the adjective ~stabilis~ (“steady, firm”), from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with French ~établir~, Italian ~stabilire~, and Portuguese ~estabelecer~; English ~establish~ was borrowed through Old French ~establir~, and its unetymological -sh reflects the Old French stressed stem.

Spanish reshaped the inherited verb with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~, “to become”), the same ending seen in ~crecer~ and ~conocer~ — so ~establecer~ literally colors “to make firm” with a sense of coming-to-stand. The e- at the front is the familiar Spanish prop-vowel that Latin ~st-~ always acquires (compare ~estar~, ~escuela~). All of this rests on the great PIE root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the most productive in the language: from it Spanish also has ~estable~, ~estabilidad~, ~establecimiento~, ~estado~, and ~estar~ itself.
en.estar:
From Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Italic *~stāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~stare~ and Portuguese ~estar~, and — through the same root — with English ~stand~ and ~stay~ and French ~ester~, an Old French verb now surviving only as a legal term.

Spanish inherited two verbs from Latin's copula system and split the work of “to be” between them: ~ser~ (from ~esse~, reinforced by ~sedēre~, “to sit”) carries permanent, essential being, while ~estar~ (from ~stāre~, “to stand”) carries location, state, and condition — literally, how something “stands” at a given moment. That is why someone ~es~ tall but ~está~ tired. The past participle ~estado~ (“been; state”) gave the noun ~estado~ (“state, condition,” and by extension the political “State”). The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ seeded a vast family of Spanish words, among them ~estación~, ~estable~, ~estatua~, ~constante~, ~restar~, and ~estatuto~.
en.estudiar:
Spanish ~estudiar~ comes from Latin ~studiāre~ (also read as a denominal from ~studium~, “zeal, application, study”), which belongs to the verb ~studeō~ (“to be eager, to apply oneself”). That verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~studēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)tewd-~ (“to push, thrust”), an extension of *~(s)tew-~ (“to push, hit”) — so its Latin sibling is ~tundō~ (“to beat, strike”). It is cognate with Italian ~studiare~, French ~étudier~ and Portuguese ~estudar~, and, as a borrowing from Old French, with English ~study~; through the deeper root it even touches English ~stub~ (“to strike, knock”).

The surprise is in that root: to study was once, at bottom, to push hard. Latin ~studeō~ meant an eager, driving zeal — a shoving of oneself toward a goal — and ~studium~ named that ardor before it ever named schoolwork. Only in late and medieval Latin did the “zeal” narrow to intellectual application, “to study.” The old heat still flickers in English ~studious~ and in Spanish ~estudioso~. The family the verb heads in Spanish is large and familiar: ~estudio~ (“study, studio”), ~estudiante~ (“student”), ~estudiantil~ (“student-related”), and ~estudioso~ (“studious; a scholar”) — every one of them descended from a word that first meant sheer eager pushing.
en.evitar:
Spanish ~evitar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēvītāre~ (“to shun, avoid”), a compound of ~ē-~/~ex-~ (“out, away”) and ~vītāre~ (“to avoid, evade”). The origin of ~vītāre~ is genuinely uncertain, and the sources disagree: by one account (De Vaan) it rests on an unattested *~vītus~ (“avoiding”), linked to Proto-Indo-European *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase, pursue”); others connect it instead to *~weyk-~ (“to yield”), or to the root of ~dīvidō~ (“to divide”). None of these is settled. Its Romance kin are straightforward: French ~éviter~, Italian ~evitare~, Portuguese ~evitar~.

Whatever its deep root, ~vītāre~ already meant in Latin “to keep clear of,” and the prefix ~ē-~ (“away”) reinforces the sense of drawing back from something — so ~evitar~ has meant “to avoid, prevent, spare” throughout its Spanish life. Because the verb entered Spanish as a learned Latinism rather than by the slow mouth-worn route of inheritance, it kept its Latin shape almost unchanged, and its Spanish family is correspondingly small and transparent: chiefly the adjectives ~evitable~ (“avoidable”) and its negation ~inevitable~ (“unavoidable”), with the adverb ~inevitablemente~. The lesson of ~evitar~ is a quieter one: not every common verb comes with a tidy prehistory, and an honest etymology sometimes ends in a shrug.
en.exigir:
From Latin ~exigere~ (“to drive out, demand, exact, weigh precisely”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, lead, do”). ~agere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), making it cognate with Ancient Greek ~ἄγω~ (ágō, “I lead”) and Sanskrit ~ajati~ (“drives”). The Latin verb descends in parallel as Italian ~esigere~, French ~exiger~ and Portuguese ~exigir~.

The core image is forceful: to ~exigere~ was to drive a debt out of someone, to exact what was owed, and Spanish ~exigir~ keeps that insistence in “to demand, to require”. A quieter branch meant “to weigh out exactly”, which is why the past participle ~exactus~ yielded ~exacto~ (“exact”), and why Latin ~examen~ (“the tongue of a balance”) gave both “swarm” and, through “a weighing”, English ~exam~. Spanish adds ~exigente~ and ~exigencia~, while ~agere~ underlies ~acto~, ~agente~ and ~ágil~; English took ~exact~, ~exigent~, ~act~ and ~agent~ from the same stock.
en.existir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~exsistere~ (also ~existere~, “to step forth, emerge, come into being”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out, forth”) and ~sistere~ (“to stand, take a stand”), a reduplicated form of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~esistere~, French ~exister~, and Portuguese ~existir~, and — through ~sistere~ and ~stāre~ — with English ~exist~, ~insist~, ~resist~, and ~consist~, and with Spanish ~estar~.

The image hidden in ~existir~ is startlingly physical: to exist is to “stand forth,” to step out of the background into visibility. Latin ~exsistere~ first meant to emerge or come into view, and only from there did it settle into the abstract “to be.” Because it is a bookish, late-arriving word — not a battered popular inheritance — it kept its Latin shape almost intact. It supplies philosophy's most famous first person, Descartes' ~existo~ in “pienso, luego ~existo~” (“I think, therefore I am”). From it Spanish built ~existencia~ (“existence”), ~existente~, ~existencial~ and ~existencialismo~, plus ~inexistente~ (“nonexistent”) and ~coexistir~ (“to coexist”).
en.explicar:
Spanish ~explicar~ comes from Latin ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, unroll, unravel”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Through that root it is cognate with Greek ~plékō~ (“I plait, weave”) and German ~flechten~ (“to braid”). To explain, then, was to unfold something rolled up — to spread a folded scroll open so it could be read.

The root ~plicāre~ was extraordinarily productive. Prefixed, it gave ~aplicar~ (“to apply”), ~implicar~ (“to implicate”), ~complicar~ (“to complicate”) and ~replicar~ (“to reply”); inherited by regular sound change it became ~plegar~ (“to fold”). Its most surprising Spanish descendant is ~llegar~ (“to arrive”): from Latin ~applicāre~ (~ad-~ + ~plicāre~), which in the peninsula's seafaring usage meant to bring a ship to shore — so “to fold in to land” became simply “to arrive.” Also here: ~pliegue~ (“fold, crease”).
en.exponer:
From Latin ~exponere~ (“to set forth, put out, display”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, place”). ~ponere~ is traditionally parsed as ~po-~ (“away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), though its deeper Proto-Indo-European ancestry is uncertain. Spanish ~exponer~ shares its Latin source with Italian ~esporre~ and Portuguese ~expor~.

The literal sense “to place out” ran in two directions: one displays an object and one sets forth an argument, and Spanish ~exponer~ still means both “to exhibit” and “to expound”, while reflexively ~exponerse~ is “to expose oneself” to danger. The derived noun ~exposición~ likewise covers an art “exhibition” and a reasoned “exposition”. The verb ~ponere~ seeded an enormous Spanish family — ~poner~, ~componer~, ~proponer~, ~imponer~ and the noun ~posición~ — and reached English in the learned derivatives ~expose~ and ~exponent~.
en.expresar:
From Late Latin ~expressāre~, a frequentative of ~exprimere~ (“to press out, squeeze out”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), whose past participle is ~expressus~. ~premere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~premō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~pres-~ (“to press”), an extension of *~per-~ (“to strike, press”). Cognates: French ~exprimer~, Italian ~esprimere~, English ~express~; and through ~premere~, English ~press~ and ~print~.

The metaphor is physical: ~exprimere~ meant to squeeze the juice from a fruit, and from “pressing out” juice came the figurative “pressing out” of words and feelings — to express. Spanish still holds both halves as a doublet: concrete ~exprimir~ (“to squeeze a lemon”) beside abstract ~expresar~ (“to put into words”). An ~expreso~ train, and espresso coffee, are likewise “pressed,” quick. From ~premere~ Spanish also drew ~prensa~ (“press, the press”), ~imprimir~ (“to print”), ~comprimir~, and ~oprimir~.
en.facilitar:
From the adjective ~fácil~ (“easy”) with a verb-forming suffix, ~fácil~ itself from Latin ~facilis~ (“easy, feasible”), which meant literally “do-able” — from ~facere~ (“to do, to make”) plus the ending ~-ilis~. ~Facere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, do”). Spanish ~facilitar~ is cognate with Italian ~facilitare~, French ~faciliter~ and Portuguese ~facilitar~, and with English ~facilitate~ and ~facile~.

Because ~facilis~ was built as “(a thing) that can be done,” its Spanish descendant ~facilitar~ means precisely “to make do-able,” to smooth the way. Its antonym preserves the same logic in reverse: ~difícil~ is ~dis-~ plus ~facilis~, “not do-able.” The parent ~facere~ is one of the great root-verbs of Spanish, surviving above all as the everyday ~hacer~ — its Latin ~f-~ softened to ~h-~ — and branching into ~fábrica~, ~facultad~ and ~facilidad~, among many others.
en.faltar:
From Vulgar Latin *~fallitare~, a frequentative of Latin ~fallere~ (“to deceive, to trip, to fail”). The origin of ~fallere~ is uncertain, but it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)gʷʰh₂el-~ (“to stumble”); on that account it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~σφάλλω~ (sphállō, “to bring down, trip up”). The same Latin verb reached English, through Old French, in ~fail~, ~fault~ and ~false~.

The semantic drift is neat: from “to deceive” to “to disappoint or come up short” and finally to “to be missing”. Spanish ~faltar~ is now the ordinary verb for something's absence — ~falta~ un ingrediente, “an ingredient is missing” — and its noun ~falta~ means “lack”, “fault”, even a sporting “foul”. The root threw off a wide family: ~falla~, ~fallar~, ~falso~ and, most strikingly, ~fallecer~ (“to die”), which began as “to fail, to expire”. English ~fallacy~ belongs here too, another child of deceiving ~fallere~.
en.firmar:
From Latin ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, strengthen, confirm”), from the adjective ~firmus~ (“firm, strong, stable”), from Proto-Italic *~fermos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-mo-s~ (“holding”), from the root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). It is cognate with Italian ~firmare~ and Portuguese ~firmar~, and — with a striking shift — with French ~fermer~ (“to close”). It is kin to English ~firm~, ~confirm~, and ~affirm~, and, far afield, to Sanskrit ~dhárma~, “that which upholds.”

The path to “sign” runs through the law: to ~firmar~ a document was first to make it firm, to confirm and ratify it, and from ratifying an act came the act of subscribing one's name to it. French, meanwhile, took ~firmāre~ toward “to shut firmly,” yielding ~fermer~, “to close.” The Spanish family keeps the core sense of steadiness: ~firme~, ~firmeza~, ~confirmar~, ~afirmar~, the ~firmamento~ (the “firm” vault of heaven), and ~firma~, the signature itself.
en.formar:
From Latin ~formāre~ (“to shape, to fashion”), from ~forma~ (“form, shape, mold”). The deeper origin of ~forma~ is genuinely disputed: one long-standing account connects it to Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape”) by metathesis, the swapping of sounds, but scholars object that Latin shows no trace of an intermediate stage and that the required sound changes are irregular. Others reconstruct a native Proto-Indo-European source instead. Cognate with French ~former~, Italian ~formare~, and English ~form~ and ~format~.

Whatever its ultimate root, ~forma~ was one of Latin’s most productive nouns, covering shape, beauty, and pattern alike. Spanish multiplied it into ~formación~, ~fórmula~ (a diminutive, “a little form”), ~informar~ (“to give form to,” to shape into knowledge), ~transformar~, and ~uniforme~ (“of one form”). A charming survival is ~horma~, the shoemaker’s or hatmaker’s last — the wooden mold that shapes a shoe. ~horma~ is the popular, inherited descendant of ~forma~, while ~forma~ itself is the learned borrowing: a doublet in which the down-to-earth mold and the abstract idea of “form” are the same Latin word taking two roads into Spanish.
en.funcionar:
~funcionar~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~función~, from Latin ~functiō~ (accusative ~functiōnem~), “a performing, execution,” from the deponent verb ~fungī~ (“to perform, discharge, carry out”), past participle ~functus~. This goes back to Proto-Italic *~fungōr~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ (“to enjoy, make use of”), the present stem carrying a nasal infix. English borrowed ~function~; French has ~fonctionner~, Italian ~funzionare~.

In Latin ~fungī~ meant “to carry out a duty,” and ~función~ named the carrying-out itself; only in the modern age did Romance coin ~funcionar~ for machines and systems that “do their job” — which is why in Spanish an engine ~funciona~. A striking cousin: ~dēfungī~ meant “to finish, be done with,” so the one who has discharged life is the ~difunto~ (“deceased”), and death is a ~defunción~. From the “use up” sense comes ~fungible~ (goods consumed in use); everyday kin include the ~funcionario~, the civil servant who performs an office.
en.ganar:
The origin of ~ganar~ is debated. Corominas argues it descends, with Portuguese ~ganhar~, from a Gothic *~ganan~ (“to covet, desire eagerly”), akin to Old Norse ~gana~ (“to gape, yearn”) — a Germanic family whose primitive sense was “to open the mouth.” Its meaning was then crossed with a separate Romance family from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, harvest, gain”): Italian ~guadagnare~, French ~gagner~ and Catalan ~guanyar~. Corominas stresses that ~ganar~ is phonetically incompatible with ~guadagnare~, so it is not simply the same word — the tidy “all from *~waidanjan~” story is exactly what he rejects.

The “desire” origin ties the verb to Spanish ~ganas~ (“urge, desire,” as in ~tener ganas~), from the very same root — a satisfying link, though it rests on the debated Gothic etymology and should be flagged as such. The senses “to gain, earn, win” all grew from there. Modern kin include ~ganancia~ (“profit”), ~ganador~ (“winner”) and, strikingly, ~ganado~ (“livestock”) — literally “what has been gained,” a reminder of an age when wealth was counted in cattle.
en.garantizar:
From ~garante~ (“guarantor”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. ~garante~ was borrowed from French ~garant~ (“warrantor, defender”), of Germanic origin: from Frankish *~werēnt~, the present participle of a verb *~werjan~ (“to warrant, to vouch for”), tracing to the Proto-Germanic root *~war-~ (“to watch, to guard, to be aware”). The same Frankish word entered English by another door: kept with its Germanic w-, it became ~warrant~ and ~warranty~, while the Central-French gu- form gave ~guarantee~ — so ~garantizar~ and ~guarantee~ are, letter for letter across the w/gu alternation, the same word.

The Germanic idea behind the word is protection. A ~garante~ was originally the one who stood surety — who vouched for another and would answer for him — and Old French already used ~garant~ in this sense in the Chanson de Roland around 1080. From this Germanic stock Spanish built a whole legal and commercial family: ~garantía~ (“guarantee, warranty”), ~garante~, ~garantizar~, and ~garantizado~, all of them galicismos layered over older native vocabulary. English keeps the twin senses in its own doublet — a ~warrant~ authorizes and vouches, while a ~guarantee~ promises and secures — two faces of the single Frankish notion of standing good for something.
en.generar:
From Latin ~generāre~ (“to beget, to produce”), from ~genus~ (“birth, origin, kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”), one of the most fertile roots in the whole language family. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~génos~ (“race, kind”), with English ~genus~ and ~generate~, and — through Germanic — with English ~kin~ and ~kind~.

At its heart the word is about birth: to generate is to bring forth offspring, and only later, by extension, to produce anything at all — heat, electricity, income, ideas. The Latin ~genus~ meant a family or stock, which is why so much vocabulary of both kinship and classification springs from it. Spanish descendants include ~género~ (“gender, genre”), ~generación~, ~gente~ (“people,” from Latin ~gens~), ~genio~ and ~ingenio~ (the inborn talent one is “born with”), and ~degenerar~ — and, more surprisingly, ~nacer~ itself, from Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), a cousin from the very same root.
en.gustar:
Spanish ~gustar~ goes back to Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste, sample, enjoy”). Curiously, the inherited Old Spanish form was ~gostar~; modern ~gustar~ is a later reborrowing closer to the Latin, whereas Portuguese kept the inherited ~gostar~. The Latin noun ~gustus~ (“a tasting, a flavor”) comes from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵews-~ (“to taste; to choose”). Through that root ~gustar~ is cognate with English ~choose~ and with the archaic English ~gust~ (“relish, keen enjoyment”).

The remarkable Spanish development is grammatical: ~gustar~ came to mean “to be pleasing to,” so the thing tasted becomes the subject and the taster an indirect object — hence ~me gusta~ literally says “it is pleasing to me,” not “I like it.” This “to like” sense is peculiar to Ibero-Romance; the older “to taste” survives in ~degustar~ (“to taste, sample”). From the same root come ~gusto~ (“taste, pleasure”), ~gustoso~ (“tasty; glad to”) and ~disgusto~ (“displeasure, upset”).
en.haber:
Spanish ~haber~, through Old Spanish ~aver~, descends from Latin ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”), from Proto-Italic *~habēō~, and — the root is generally traced this way, though debated — from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, take, hold”). Its Romance siblings all preserve the sense of holding or possessing: French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~, Portuguese ~haver~, and Romanian ~avea~. English ~have~ looks and sounds like an obvious cousin, but it is a false friend: it belongs to the Germanic family and, as we will see, springs from an entirely different root, so the resemblance is pure coincidence.

Where French and Italian kept ~avoir~ and ~avere~ as the everyday verb of possession, Spanish demoted ~haber~ to a near-pure auxiliary and handed ownership to ~tener~ (from Latin ~tenēre~, “to hold”). Two roles remained: the auxiliary of the compound tenses (~he cantado~, “I have sung”) and the impersonal existential ~hay~, ~había~, ~habrá~ (“there is, there are”). The old possessive sense survives only fossilized, in the noun ~haber~ / ~haberes~ (“assets, wages”) and set phrases like ~habérselas con~. The form ~hay~ deserves its own note: it is medieval ~ha~ plus the locative clitic ~y~ (from Latin ~ibī~, “there”), exactly parallel to French ~il y a~ and Catalan ~hi ha~ — literally “it has there,” hence “there is.” From the same Latin verb Spanish also draws a learned family: ~hábito~, ~habitar~, ~exhibir~, ~prohibir~, and — via ~dēbēre~, that is ~dē-~ plus ~habēre~ — the verb ~deber~.

German ~haben~ completes the trap. It comes not from the root behind ~habēre~ but from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”) — the very root that in Latin produced ~capiō~ (“I seize”), and through it Spanish ~captar~, ~cautivo~, and ~aceptar~. So the two great “have” verbs of Western Europe are not related at all; they were pulled into the same shape by a ~Sprachbund~, the long convergence of neighboring languages, until each ended up an auxiliary: Spanish ~he comido~ mirrors German ~ich habe gegessen~. There is a final twist. Old Spanish did once share the European auxiliary split, taking “be” for verbs of motion and change — ~es nacido~ (“is born”), ~so venido~ (“is come”) — but it later leveled the system, generalizing ~haber~ to every compound tense (~ha muerto~, not older ~es muerto~). So modern Spanish, unlike French and German, no longer keeps the ~ser~/~haber~ division it once had. English quietly did the same: it once formed the perfect of verbs of motion and change with ~be~ — ~I am come~, ~he is risen~ — before ~have~ took over there too.
en.hablar:
From Old Spanish ~fablar~, from Latin ~fābulārī~ (“to chat, converse”), a verb built on ~fābula~ (“story, talk”), itself from ~fārī~ (“to speak”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Portuguese ~falar~ and Italian ~favellare~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~fāma~ (whence English ~fame~) and the learned English doublet ~fable~, borrowed straight from ~fābula~.

The Latin ~f~ of ~fablar~ weakened to an aspirated ~h~ in early Castilian and then fell silent, so medieval ~fablar~ became modern ~hablar~ while the letter lingered on, mute — one of the sound-changes that most sharply distinguishes Spanish from its Romance siblings. The meaning drifted too: where classical Latin used ~fābulārī~ for idle chatting, Spanish promoted it to the ordinary word for “to speak,” displacing ~loquī~. From ~fābula~ Spanish also drew the learned ~fábula~ (“fable”) and ~fabuloso~, while ~hablar~ itself seeded ~habla~ (“speech”), ~hablador~ (“chatterbox”), ~hablante~ (“speaker”), and ~hablilla~ (“rumor”).
en.hacer:
Spanish ~hacer~ comes, through Old Spanish ~fazer~, from Latin ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, set, place”). The same root gave the English verb ~do~ and German ~tun~, so ~hacer~ and ~do~ are true cousins under the skin. Its Romance siblings kept the Latin ~f-~: Italian ~fare~, French ~faire~, Portuguese ~fazer~. Spanish alone let that ~f-~ drift to a silent ~h-~, the regular change that turned ~facere~ into ~hacer~.

Latin ~facere~ was the great all-purpose verb of doing and making, and its progeny is enormous. Spanish keeps the past participle ~hecho~ (“done; fact”), and builds ~deshacer~ (“to undo”), ~satisfacer~ (“to satisfy,” literally “to make enough”), and ~hacienda~ (“estate, treasury”). Learned borrowings that skipped the ~f-~-to-~h-~ shift preserve the older look: ~factor~, ~efecto~ (“effect”), and ~factible~ (“feasible”) — a whole workshop of words for making.
en.identificar:
From Medieval Latin ~identificāre~ (“to make identical”), a compound of ~identitās~ (“sameness, identity”) and ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~identitās~ was itself a late, learned coinage from ~idem~ (“the same”). The word spread through the Romance languages as a scholarly borrowing rather than by inheritance: Italian ~identificare~, French ~identifier~, Portuguese ~identificar~, and English ~identify~ all arrived by the same learned route in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Because ~identificar~ is a bookish, relatively modern formation, its story belongs to philosophy and law rather than to folk speech. ~idem~, “the very same,” carried the Latin idea of exact sameness, and ~-ficāre~ carried “to make,” so the verb means literally “to make one and the same” — to establish that a person and a name denote a single thing. From ~idem~ Spanish also keeps ~ídem~ (the ditto word), ~identidad~, and ~idéntico~; from ~facere~ descends a whole crowd of ~-ficar~ verbs such as ~verificar~, ~clasificar~, and ~modificar~. The reflexive ~identificarse~ (“to identify oneself” — to show one's papers, or to feel kinship with someone) is a later extension, its bureaucratic and emotional senses growing up side by side.
en.implicar:
From Latin ~implicāre~ (“to fold in, entangle, involve”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, fold”). Cognate with — and in several cases borrowed as — English ~imply~, ~employ~, and ~implicate~, and French ~impliquer~.

The image is physical: to ~implicar~ is to fold something in so that it becomes entangled with something else — hence “to involve” and, of a statement, “to imply.” A quiet surprise is that Spanish ~emplear~ (“to employ, use”) is a doublet: the same ~plicāre~ reached it by a worn popular road through Old French, whereas the learned form was lifted straight from Latin. The fold-family is large: ~aplicar~ (“to apply”), ~explicar~ (“to explain,” to unfold), ~complicar~ (“to complicate”), ~plegar~ (“to fold”), and ~replicar~ (“to reply”).
en.imponer:
From Latin ~impōnere~ (“to set upon, lay on”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). ~Pōnere~ was itself a contraction of the particle ~po-~ and ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”). Spanish ~imponer~ is cognate with Italian ~imporre~ and Portuguese ~impor~; French ~imposer~ and English ~impose~ belong to the family too, though both were reshaped on the participle stem ~positus~ rather than the infinitive.

The literal “place upon” quickly turned figurative: to ~imponer~ is to lay a tax, a rule, or a penalty on someone, and reflexively ~imponerse~ is to assert oneself or prevail. The participle ~impositus~ gave the popular ~impuesto~, which in Spanish is not only “imposed” but the everyday noun “tax.” The parent ~pōnere~ founded one of Spanish's largest verb families — ~poner~, ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~ — each pairing a learned noun in ~-posición~ with a popular participle in ~-puesto~, as in ~composición~ beside ~compuesto~.
en.incluir:
A semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~inclūdere~ (“to shut in, enclose”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, shut”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg; to close”). Cognate with Italian ~includere~, French ~inclure~, and Portuguese ~incluir~, and — through ~claudere~ — with English ~include~, ~conclude~, ~exclude~, and ~close~, plus Latin ~clāvis~ (“key,” whence Spanish ~llave~ and ~clave~).

That ~incluir~ is only semi-learned shows in its shape: a fully popular descent would have battered the word far more, but scholars and scribes reintroduced it close to the Latin, keeping the combining form ~-clūdere~ (with the ~au~ of ~claudere~ raised to ~ū~). The literal image is spatial — to shut something inside — from which the modern “to contain, comprise, include” follows directly. The same ~claudere~ radiates through Spanish ~concluir~, ~excluir~, and ~recluir~, and ~inclūdere~ itself yields ~inclusión~, the adverb ~incluso~ (“even, including”), and ~inclusivo~ (“inclusive”).
en.incorporar:
From Latin ~incorporāre~ (“to form into a body, embody”), from ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~corpus~ (stem ~corpor-~, “body”) plus the verbal suffix ~-āre~. ~Corpus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~korpos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~krep-~ (“body, form”). Cognate with French ~incorporer~ and English ~incorporate~; the root itself is shared with English ~midriff~, from Old English ~hrif~ (“belly”).

The literal sense is “to put into a body,” to make separate things into one mass — it is the verb for folding egg whites into a batter, and the reason a company is “incorporated” into one legal body. Spanish ~incorporarse~ also means to sit or stand up, to bring the body upright. From ~corpus~ Spanish inherited ~cuerpo~ (“body”), ~corporal~, ~corpóreo~, ~corporación~, ~corpiño~ (“bodice”), and — by a French detour — ~corsé~ (“corset”).
en.indicar:
From Latin ~indicāre~ (“to point out, show, declare”), from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim, dedicate”), a cousin of ~dīcere~ (“to say”); all go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deik-~ (“to show, point out”). It is cognate with Italian ~indicare~, Portuguese ~indicar~ and French ~indiquer~, and with English ~indicate~ and ~index~; through Germanic the same root gives English ~teach~ and ~token~.

Where ~dicāre~ was “to proclaim aloud,” ~indicāre~ was “to point a finger at,” and the finger is not incidental: the ~índice~ (“index finger”) is literally the pointer, and an ~índice~ in a book points you to its contents. From *~deik-~ Spanish gathers a wide family — ~indicio~ (“clue”), ~indicador~ (“indicator”), ~dedicar~ (“to dedicate,” from ~dēdicāre~) and ~predicar~ (“to preach,” from ~praedicāre~) — while Latin ~digitus~ (“finger”), from the same root, underlies ~dígito~ and English ~digit~.
en.informar:
From Latin ~informāre~ (“to give shape to, to form, to describe, to instruct”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into”) and ~formāre~ (“to form, to shape”), from the noun ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”). The origin of ~forma~ is genuinely uncertain: it has long been proposed to derive from Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape, form”) by metathesis, perhaps mediated by Etruscan, but the account is disputed and remains unproven, so the deeper source is best left open. The verb carried into Italian ~informare~, French ~informer~, and English ~inform~.

The literal sense is “to put into form,” and the abstract senses grew straight out of it: to shape the mind (“to instruct”), to shape an account (“to describe, to report”), and at last “to inform.” The very word “information” is, at root, a shaping of the mind. A charming doublet hides in the family: Spanish ~forma~ and ~horma~ (a shoemaker's “last” or mold) are the same Latin ~forma~ — one learned, one popularly inherited with ~f~ turned to ~h~. Alongside them stand ~formar~, ~fórmula~, ~formal~, ~transformar~, ~reformar~, and ~uniforme~.
en.iniciar:
From Latin ~initiāre~ (“to begin, to initiate into”), from ~initium~ (“a beginning, an entrance”), from ~inīre~ (“to go in, to enter”), which is ~in-~ (“into”) + ~īre~ (“to go”). ~īre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~eō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root shared with Sanskrit ~éti~ (“he goes”) and Ancient Greek ~eîmi~ (“I will go”). Spanish borrowed the learned ~iniciar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~iniziare~, French ~initier~, and Portuguese ~iniciar~.

In Rome ~initiāre~ carried a solemn charge beyond “to begin”: it meant to admit someone into the ~initium~ — the entrance, the threshold — of the mystery religions, to initiate them into secret rites. Spanish ~iniciar~ preserves both the everyday “to start” and this ceremonial “to initiate.” The going-root *~h₁ey-~ is faint in Spanish because ~īre~ was largely replaced, but it still shows in ~ir~ (whose forms mix three Latin verbs), ~inicio~, ~iniciativa~, ~éxito~ (“a going-out,” hence “success”), and ~tránsito~.
en.instalar:
From French ~installer~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~installare~, a compound of Latin ~in-~ (“in”) and ~stallum~ (“stall, seat”). ~stallum~ was itself taken from a Germanic word for a standing-place or stable, Frankish *~stall~, from Proto-Germanic *~stallaz~, traceable to the Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to put, stand”). The Germanic noun surfaces directly in English ~stall~ and German ~Stall~ (“stable”).

The medieval verb was strikingly concrete: to ~installare~ a canon or official was to seat him in his ~stallum~ — the assigned stall or choir seat that marked his office. From “to place someone in his seat” the meaning widened to “to set anything in its proper place”, and modern Spanish ~instalar~ ranges from installing a person in a post to installing plumbing or software. Spanish keeps the family in ~instalación~ and ~instalador~, while the same Germanic root gave English ~stall~, ~stallion~ and ~forestall~.
en.integrar:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, to renew”), from the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, untouched, intact”), from Proto-Italic *~n̥tagros~ (“untouched”): the negative prefix ~in-~ (“not”) joined to the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch”). Something ~integer~ was, literally, un-touched. English borrowed the same Latin adjective as ~integer~ and ~entire~, and the root surfaces again in the borrowed ~tangent~ and ~tact~; the Italian ~integrare~ and French ~intégrer~ descend from the same verb.

Latin ~integrāre~ meant “to make whole again, to renew, to restore,” and that sense of completing and unifying carried into Spanish ~integrar~ (“to integrate, to make up, to compose”). The idea of the untouched-and-therefore-whole also gave Spanish a pair of doublets from the same ~integer~: the learned ~íntegro~ (“upright, complete”) and the inherited ~entero~ (“entire, whole”). From the “touch” root came a wide family — ~integridad~, ~integración~, and, through ~tangere~, the words ~tacto~, ~contacto~, ~intacto~, ~tangente~ and ~contagio~.
en.intentar:
From Latin ~intentāre~ (“to stretch toward, to aim at”), a frequentative of ~intendere~ (“to direct, to focus one's attention”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) plus ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tendō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~tend-~, a d-extension of the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through that root it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~, Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and English ~thin~, ~tend~, and ~tense~. Italian ~intentare~ and Portuguese ~intentar~ preserve the same compound.

The frequentative suffix once painted a repeated, insistent stretching-toward, and from that intensified aiming the sense narrowed to “to attempt, to try.” Spanish also kept a legal and rhetorical use, where ~intentar~ una demanda means “to bring a suit.” The prolific root *~ten-~ seeded a wide family in Spanish, among them ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a “tent,” and hence a “shop”), ~tensión~, ~intención~, ~atender~, ~extender~, and ~contender~.
en.interesar:
From ~interés~ (“interest”), a noun Spanish took from Latin ~interest~ (“it matters, it concerns”), the third-person form of the verb ~interesse~ (“to be between, to be present at, to concern”). That verb joins ~inter-~ (“between, among”) to ~esse~ (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”), the same root behind Spanish ~ser~ and ~es~. Spanish ~interesar~ is cognate with Italian ~interessare~, French ~intéresser~ and English ~interest~, all descending from that Latin idiom for something that “lies between” the parties and therefore concerns them.

The semantic journey is a small lesson in economics and psychology alike. What “is between” people was, in Roman law, what mattered to them — a stake, a share, a concern. From that came the financial ~interés~ (the “concern” a lender holds in a loan, hence the money it earns) and, in parallel, the mental ~interés~, the attention we give to what concerns us. The reflexive ~interesarse~ (“to take an interest”) captures the second sense, while ~interesado~ can mean both “interested” and, less flatteringly, “self-interested.” Kin through ~esse~ include ~esencia~, ~ausente~, ~presente~ and ~interesante~ itself.
en.ir:
Spanish ~ir~ is, like ~ser~, a patchwork of several Latin verbs. Its infinitive and future come from Latin ~īre~ (“to go”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root also visible in Greek ~eîmi~ (“I go”) and Sanskrit ~éti~. But the present tense (~voy~, ~vas~, ~va~, ~van~) comes instead from a different Latin verb, ~vādere~ (“to walk, advance”), and the preterite (~fui~, ~fue~) is borrowed wholesale from ~esse~, the perfect ~fuī~ that ~ser~ also uses.

So a single tiny verb draws on three sources — ~īre~ for the infinitive, ~vādere~ for the present, ~fuī~ for the past — one of the most thoroughly suppletive verbs in the language. The shared preterite is the memorable twist: ~fui~ means both “I went” and “I was,” the two verbs indistinguishable in that tense, context alone deciding. The ~vādere~ strand seeded further Spanish words — ~invadir~ (“to invade,” to go in), ~evadir~ (“to evade,” to go out), and ~vadear~ (“to ford”) — while ~īre~ itself left little behind but this one indispensable verb.
en.jugar:
From Latin ~iocāre~, a Vulgar-Latin variant of ~iocārī~ (“to jest, to play”), from ~iocus~ (“joke, jest”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yek-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Italian ~giocare~, French ~jouer~, and Portuguese ~jogar~, and — through the same ~iocus~ — with English ~joke~ and ~juggle~ (the latter from Latin ~ioculārī~).

The surprise is that play began as talk. ~iocus~ was originally a spoken jest — the PIE root *~yek-~ means “to speak” — so the earliest “play” was word-play, banter, a joke. Only later did Spanish broaden ~jugar~ to cover games, sport, and gambling of every kind, leaving the verbal sense to ~bromear~. The old root still shows in ~jocoso~ (“humorous, jocular”), which kept close to the original joking. Everyday relatives include ~juego~ (“game, play”), ~jugador~ (“player”), and ~juguete~ (“toy”) — the whole vocabulary of fun grown from a single spoken quip.
en.lanzar:
From Old Spanish ~lançar~, from Late Latin ~lanceāre~ (“to wield or hurl a lance”), from Latin ~lancea~ (“lance, light spear”). The origin of ~lancea~ itself is disputed: the Roman writer Varro reported it as a foreign, Hispanic word, so it is often traced to a Celtic or Iberian source — but the details are uncertain and no reconstruction is secure. Cognate with Italian ~lanciare~, French ~lancer~, and — borrowed through Old French — English ~lance~ and ~launch~.

The semantic path is neat: from a specific act, “to thrust with a lance,” Latin ~lanceāre~ broadened to any forceful throwing, and Spanish ~lanzar~ now covers hurling a ball, launching a rocket, or bringing a product to market. English ~launch~ took the very same journey through French. From ~lancea~ Spanish keeps the noun ~lanza~ (“lance”), ~lance~ (“incident, cast”), ~lanzamiento~ (“throw, launch”), and ~lanzadera~ (“shuttle”).
en.leer:
From Latin ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick out, to choose, to read”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). Cognate with Italian ~leggere~, French ~lire~, and Portuguese ~ler~; the Greek branch, ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), yielded ~lógos~ and the whole ~-logy~ family. Through Latin the same root gives English ~lecture~, ~legible~, ~legend~, ~collect~, and ~elect~.

The oldest sense was physical — ~legere~ meant to gather up or pick out, as one gathers firewood or picks grapes. “To read” is a metaphor grown from it: the eye gathers the scattered letters and picks out the words, one by one. Greek made the parallel leap from “gathering” to “speaking,” which is how a word for collecting became ~lógos~, “word, reason.” Spanish narrowed ~leer~ to reading alone but keeps the gathering sense in ~elegir~ (“to choose”) and ~colegir~ (“to infer, to gather”), plus the reading cluster ~lección~, ~lectura~, ~legible~, and ~leyenda~ (“legend,” literally “things to be read”).
en.levantar:
From Vulgar Latin *~levantāre~, built on ~levāns~ (stem ~levant-~), the present participle of Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, lift, lighten”), from ~levis~ (“light in weight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~levantar~ and, through ~levāre~, with French ~lever~ and Italian ~levare~; through ~levis~ it is kin to English ~light~ (not heavy) and even ~lung~, the “light” organ that floats.

The base ~levāre~ meant both “to make lighter” and “to raise up,” and the frequentative ending gave ~levantar~ its brisk sense of lifting and getting up. Two descendants preserve a vivid picture: ~Levante~, the East, is the quarter where the sun “raises itself,” and ~levadura~ (“leaven, yeast”) is what makes dough rise. The wider family includes ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to lighten, relieve”), ~leve~, ~liviano~, and ~levantamiento~ (“uprising”) — all turning on the double idea of lightness and rising.
en.limitar:
From Latin ~limitare~ (“to mark off, set bounds”), formed from ~limes~ (genitive ~limitis~), “a boundary, a cross-path between fields, a frontier”. ~limes~ is usually derived from ~limus~ (“sidelong, transverse”) and set beside ~limen~ (“threshold”), though the exact relationship among these words is debated. It descends in Italian ~limitare~, French ~limiter~ and Portuguese ~limitar~.

The Roman ~limes~ began as the balk or path running crosswise between plots, then hardened into something grander: the fortified ~limes~ that marked the edge of the empire, from the German frontier to Hadrian's Wall. To ~limitare~ was to trace such a boundary, and Spanish ~limitar~ still means both “to set a limit” and “to border on” a neighbour. The family includes ~límite~, ~limítrofe~ (“bordering”) and ~limitación~, and English drew ~limit~ and ~limitation~ straight from the same Latin, while the neighbouring ~limen~ surfaces in English ~liminal~.
en.llamar:
From Old Spanish ~clamar~, from Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out, shout”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Italian ~chiamare~, French ~clamer~, and Portuguese ~chamar~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~calāre~ (“to call out”) and the English borrowings ~claim~ and ~clamor~.

The initial Latin cluster ~cl-~ palatalized to the Spanish ~ll-~ (the same shift that turned ~clāvem~ into ~llave~ and ~plēnum~ into ~lleno~), so ~clāmāre~ yielded popular ~llamar~ while a learned ~clamar~ (“to clamor, cry out”) was later re-borrowed alongside it. The sense softened from the urgency of shouting to the everyday acts of calling, summoning, and — reflexively, in ~llamarse~ — being named: one no longer cries out a name but simply ~se llama~ it. The root also gave Spanish ~clamor~, ~reclamar~ (“to claim, demand”), and ~exclamar~, plus the derivatives ~llamada~ (“call”), ~llamamiento~ (“summons”), and ~llamativo~ (“eye-catching”).
en.llegar:
From Old Spanish ~llegar~, from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”) — or, by a competing account, from its compound ~applicāre~ (“to bring to, to land a ship”), the initial ~a-~ later lost. Either way the ~pl-~ hardened into Spanish ~ll-~. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Portuguese ~chegar~ came the same way; the folding sense stayed put in the learned doublet ~plegar~ and in Italian ~piegare~ and French ~plier~; English ~ply~ and ~apply~ are relatives.

How “to fold” became “to arrive” is debated. The usual explanation is nautical — a ship reaching harbor folds its sails, or is brought folded up against the shore — fitting for the seafaring peninsula, though it remains a proposal rather than a proven fact. Strikingly, the very same Latin verb went the opposite way in Romanian ~pleca~ (“to leave, to depart”), by one account from folding up a tent to move on — so a single root yielded both “arrive” and “leave.” Spanish derivatives include ~llegada~ (“arrival”) and the doublet family of ~plegar~, ~aplicar~, ~replicar~, and ~complicar~.
en.llevar:
From Old Spanish ~levar~, from Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, to lift”), from the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”) — the same root that gave English its native ~light~. The Romance siblings are Italian ~levare~, French ~lever~, and Portuguese ~levar~; English also took the learned ~lever~, ~elevate~, ~alleviate~, and ~relieve~ from the same Latin stock.

The path from “to lift” to Spanish ~llevar~ (“to carry, to take, to wear”) runs through the natural chain of lifting a load, then bearing it, then bearing it away. Spanish split the work with a cousin: ~llevar~ carries something from here to there, while ~traer~ brings it toward the speaker. The plainer sense of “to raise” stayed with the doublet ~levantar~ (“to lift, to raise”), and the family also yields ~leve~ (“light, slight”), ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to relieve”), ~relevar~ (“to relieve, to relay”), and ~sublevar~ (“to incite to revolt”).
en.lograr:
From Latin ~lucrārī~ (“to gain, to profit”), a deponent verb from the noun ~lucrum~ (“gain, profit, wealth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂w-~ (“to seize, to gain”). The same root surfaces in Germanic as Proto-Germanic *~launą~ (“reward”), giving German ~Lohn~ (“wage”) and Old English ~lēan~ (“reward”), and in Greek ~apolaúō~ (“to enjoy”). Within Romance, Spanish ~lograr~ stands beside the learned borrowing ~lucro~ and its Portuguese and Italian relatives.

The meaning traveled a satisfying road. Latin ~lucrārī~ was mercantile — to turn a profit — and Old Spanish ~lograr~ first meant “to enjoy or possess” something, to have the benefit of it. From “enjoying the gain” the verb slid to “obtaining the desired thing” and finally to today’s “to achieve, to manage to.” The word’s history is thus its own small success story: from raw profit, through enjoyment, to accomplishment. Alongside the popular ~lograr~ Spanish keeps the doublet ~logro~ (“achievement,” and formerly “usury, interest”), plus the learned ~lucro~ and ~lucrativo~, which stayed close to the original money-making sense.
en.manifestar:
From Latin ~manifestare~ (“to make plain, reveal”), derived from the adjective ~manifestus~ (“caught in the act, flagrant, evident, palpable”). Its first element is clearly ~manus~ (“hand”); the second is disputed — it may descend from a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰers-~ (“to be bold”), itself from *~dʰer-~ (“to hold”), but the analysis is uncertain and no confident sense can be assigned. Latin passed the verb to Italian ~manifestare~, French ~manifester~ and Portuguese ~manifestar~.

Whatever its build, ~manifestus~ evoked something so palpable it could almost be taken in the hand — a wrongdoer “caught red-handed”, a fact plain to all. Spanish ~manifestar~ accordingly means “to show, reveal, declare”, and reflexively ~manifestarse~ is “to demonstrate”, to make one's views public in the street. Hence the noun ~manifestación~ (“demonstration, manifestation”) and ~manifiesto~ (“manifesto”). The transparent first element ~manus~ anchors a huge Spanish family — ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~mantener~ — and English borrowed the verb's own offspring in ~manifest~ and ~manifesto~.
en.mantener:
From Latin ~manū~ ~tenēre~, literally “to hold in the hand,” a phrase of ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”) that fused into Vulgar Latin ~manutenēre~. The second element, shared with ~tener~, goes back to Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”); the first, ~manus~, comes from Proto-Italic *~manus~ and *~man-~ (“hand”). Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~mantenere~, Portuguese ~manter~ and French ~maintenir~; English ~maintain~ is the same compound, borrowed through Old French ~maintenir~.

The image is concrete: to “hold in the hand” became to keep, support, sustain and maintain — the range Spanish ~mantener~ still spans, from ~mantener~ una promesa to ~mantener~ a la familia. Its ~tenēre~ half anchors a huge family — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~detener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while ~manus~ gives ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~maniobra~ (“maneuver,” from ~manū~ ~operāre~, “to work by hand”). Through the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) ~mantener~ is even distantly kin to ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a stretched tent-shop) and English ~tenant~ and ~tension~.
en.marcar:
Spanish ~marcar~ (“to mark”) has a debated immediate history: it is either a native formation from the noun ~marca~ (“mark, boundary”) plus the verb-ending ~-ar~, or a loan from Italian ~marcare~ (“to put a mark on”). Either way the deeper source is Germanic. The noun ~marca~ goes back, through Medieval Latin ~marca~, to Proto-Germanic *~markō~ (“boundary, borderland, region”), which entered Ibero-Romance from a Germanic tongue — Gothic or Frankish. So the root idea is not a scribble but a border. It is cognate with Italian ~marca~, German ~Mark~ and English ~mark~ and ~march~ (“borderland”).

The semantic path runs from the land inward. A ~marca~ was first a frontier district — the borderlands a ruler had to guard — which is exactly why medieval marches gave us titles like “marquis” (Spanish ~marqués~), the lord set over a ~marca~. From “boundary” the noun narrowed to the “mark” one sets to claim or delimit, and the verb ~marcar~ to the act of making such a mark — on cattle, on a page, on a scoreboard. Its Spanish kin spread across that whole span: ~marco~ (“frame”), ~marcador~ (“marker; scoreboard”), ~comarca~ (“district,” literally land within borders), ~demarcar~ (“to demarcate”) and ~marcapasos~ (“pacemaker”).
en.mejorar:
Spanish ~mejorar~ comes from Late Latin ~meliōrāre~ (“to make better”), a verb built on the Latin comparative ~melior~ (“better”). ~melior~ is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~mel-~ (“strong, great”), the same root credited with Latin ~multus~ (“much”) and Ancient Greek ~μάλα~ (mála, “very”). Its Romance reflexes are everywhere: the adjective survives as Spanish ~mejor~, Portuguese ~melhor~, French ~meilleur~, and Italian ~migliore~, and the verb as Portuguese ~melhorar~ and Italian ~migliorare~. English ~ameliorate~ borrowed the Latin verb through French.

There is a small surprise in ~mejor~: it serves as the comparative of ~bueno~ (“good”) yet shares no root with it. Latin ~bonus~ lacked a comparative of its own and borrowed ~melior~ from an unrelated word — the pattern called suppletion, the same quirk behind English “good/better.” So ~mejorar~ means, transparently, to make or become better. From the root Spanish keeps ~mejor~, ~mejora~ (“improvement”), ~mejoría~ (“recovery”), and ~mejoramiento~; through the cognate ~multus~ come ~mucho~, ~muy~, ~multitud~, and ~múltiple~.
en.mencionar:
From ~mención~ (“mention”), a learned noun taken from Latin ~mentiō~ (stem ~mentiōn-~, “a calling to mind, a naming”), which grows from the same root as ~meminī~ (“to remember”) and ~mēns~ (“mind”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). The verb ~mencionar~ is cognate with French ~mentionner~, Italian ~menzionare~ and English ~mention~; through the shared root *~men-~ it is also kin to English ~mind~ and ~mental~.

Latin ~mentiō~ literally named the act of bringing something back to mind, and Spanish kept that thread: to ~mencionar~ is to summon a thing into speech, to call it to notice. Older and more colloquial is the inherited doublet ~mentar~ (“to name, to bring up”), alive in the blunt phrase ~mentar~ la madre. From the same root *~men-~ Spanish drew a broad cognitive vocabulary — ~mente~ (“mind”), ~mental~, ~memoria~, ~comentar~ (“to comment”) and ~mentor~ — and, by one account, even ~mentir~ (“to lie”), as though a falsehood were merely something thought up; but that last link is debated.
en.meter:
From Old Spanish ~meter~, from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”). The deeper origin is uncertain; by one account ~mittere~ traces to Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), an extension of the root *~mey-~ (“to change”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~meter~, Italian ~mettere~, and French ~mettre~.

In Latin ~mittere~ meant “to send,” but already in Vulgar Latin the sense drifted toward “to put, place, insert,” which is what Spanish ~meter~ means today — you ~meter~ a key into a lock or a hand into a pocket. The learned family stayed closer to the original “send”: ~admitir~, ~remitir~, ~prometer~, and ~someter~ all preserve the Latin verb. From its participle ~missus~ came a cluster of everyday nouns: ~misión~ (“a sending”), ~mensaje~ (“message”), and ~remesa~ (“remittance, shipment”). Even ~misa~ (“Mass”) belongs here, from ~missa~ in the dismissal formula that once closed the service. English ~mission~ and ~message~ are cousins from the same Latin verb.
en.mirar:
From Latin ~mīrārī~ (“to wonder at, to marvel”), a deponent verb formed on the adjective ~mīrus~ (“wonderful, astonishing”). ~mīrus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~smeiros~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)mey-~ (“to smile, to be glad”) — so, remarkably, ~mirar~ is a blood relative of English ~smile~ and of Sanskrit ~sméra~ (“smiling”). Italian ~mirare~, French ~mirer~, and Portuguese ~mirar~ share the inheritance.

Here the surprise is a loss: Latin ~mīrārī~ was charged with astonishment, but everyday Spanish ~mirar~ drained the wonder away until it meant simply “to look at, to watch.” The amazement did not vanish, though — it took refuge in the learned offspring ~admirar~, ~milagro~ (from ~mīrāculum~), and ~maravilla~ (from ~mīrābilia~, “wonders”). English drew from the same well for ~admire~, ~miracle~, ~marvel~, and — through Vulgar Latin's “to look at” — ~mirror~, the glass you gaze into. Spanish adds ~mirada~, ~mirador~, and ~mira~.
en.morir:
From Vulgar Latin *~morīre~, a regularization of Classical Latin ~morī~ (“to die,” a deponent verb), from Proto-Indo-European *~mer-~ (“to die”). Cognate with Italian ~morire~, French ~mourir~ and Portuguese ~morrer~; through the root, with Sanskrit ~mṛtyú~ (“death”), Ancient Greek ~brotós~ (“mortal”) and — via Germanic — English ~murder~.

Classical ~morī~ was deponent (passive in form, active in meaning); Vulgar Latin recast it as an ordinary verb *~morīre~, the ancestor of every Romance form. From the participle ~mortuus~ and the noun ~mors~ (stem ~mort-~) came Spanish ~muerte~, ~muerto~, ~mortal~, ~moribundo~ and ~amortiguar~.
